reading.title: How Strange Results Push Science Forward
reading.purpose: Explore how careful testing and unexpected anomalies reshape scientific theories.
paras: In daily talk, people sometimes say "just a theory" to mean a wild guess. In science, a theory is the exact reverse. It is a well-tested model backed by mountains of empirical proof from direct sight and lab tests. For years, teams work inside a shared paradigm, a set of core ideas and tools that guides how a field asks questions and reads data.

To keep findings strong, tests must be rigorous—thorough, exact, and strict enough to rule out sloppy slips. Teams gather both quantitative data, such as exact heat or grams weighed on a scale, and qualitative notes on color, feel, or smell. They also watch for stray factors that could confound a test, sneaking in an unplanned shift so no one can tell what truly caused the result.

Proving causation—showing that one factor truly makes another happen—takes more than one lucky day. Outside labs try to replicate the test, repeating the exact steps to see if the same result shows up again. When three labs in three lands get the same counts, trust climbs fast.

Now and then, a careful test turns up an anomaly, an odd reading that refuses to fit the known pattern. Rather than hiding that strange point, good teams study it. At times the flaw is a dusty probe; at other times, the odd reading forces the whole field to rethink its model. In science, trust is earned one checked test at a time.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "anomaly" most nearly means
choices: a measurement that fails to fit the expected pattern
a lab scale used to record exact weights in grams
a well-tested explanation shared by three countries
a notebook describing the color and texture of rocks
qs.why: Paragraph 4 defines anomaly directly as "an unexpected measurement that refuses to fit the reigning pattern."

qs.q: Which sentence shows the difference between numerical measurements and descriptive observations?
choices: To keep findings strong, tests must be rigorous—thorough, exact, and strict enough to rule out sloppy slips.

qs.why: This sentence contrasts quantitative data (heat, grams) with qualitative notes (color, feel, smell).

ev.text: Teams gather both quantitative data, such as exact heat or grams weighed on a scale, and qualitative notes on color, feel, or smell.

qs.q: Why do independent labs try to replicate an experiment?
choices: To verify that repeating the same steps produces the same result reliably.
To replace all quantitative data with easier qualitative descriptions.
To hide any dusty sensors or unplanned variables from other scientists.
To prove that everyday hunches are just as strong as tested theories.
qs.why: Paragraph 3 states that independent labs replicate an experiment "to check whether the same result appears again," which builds confidence.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Dusty sensors are the main reason most scientific theories have to be thrown away.
Scientific knowledge grows stronger through rigorous testing, replication, and investigating unexpected results.
Qualitative notes about odor and texture are less valuable than exact numbers on a scale.
Once a paradigm is accepted by a field, scientists should ignore any strange readings.
qs.why: The reading explains how empirical evidence, rigorous controls, replication, and investigating anomalies keep science reliable and self-correcting.
